summary: Specifies a shared LISP message type for future extensions and experiments, and a registry for packet types. It updates RFC 6830. Replaced by RFC 9304.

eli5.summary: One flexible mailbox for new ideas instead of a new box each time.

questions: what is lisp shared extension message
how do lisp packet types work
subtitle: One flexible message type for LISP extensions instead of allocating a new type for each.

tldr.problem: The LISP protocol defined only 16 possible packet type codes, but many extensions needed new types. Allocating a unique type for each extension would quickly exhaust the limited space.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC reserves one shared message type (type 15) and uses sub-types (0-4095) within that type to identify specific extensions, allowing many more extensions to coexist. It also creates an IANA registry for LISP packet types.
tldr.outcome: Extensions can now share a single packet type with unique sub-type identifiers, preserving the packet type space. This RFC was later updated by RFC 9304.

today: RFC 9304 updated and superseded this RFC with further refinements to LISP message handling. The shared extension message mechanism remains in use for LISP experimental features and extensions.

sections.title: Problem and Solution
sections.content:
The Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP), defined in RFC 6830, uses packet type codes (0-15) to identify different message types. The base protocol reserves codes for Map-Request, Map-Reply, Map-Register, Map-Notify, and Encapsulated Control Messages. This leaves limited space for extensions.

Several LISP extensions have been proposed (LISP-DDT, LISP-MN-EXT, LISP-BULK, NAT-LISP, LISP-SUBSCRIBE), and more are expected. Rather than allocate one type code for each extension (which would exhaust the 16-code space), this RFC designates one message type as a shared extension type and introduces sub-types to distinguish between extensions.
sections.eli5: LISP messages come in different types, numbered 0-15. But there are many new ideas for LISP features, and you can't have more than 16 types. The solution: use type 15 for 'new experiments,' and put a sticker on each one to say which experiment.

sections.title: The Shared Extension Message Format
sections.content:
The LISP shared extension message uses type code 15. The message begins with a standard 32-bit header field: the Type (4 bits) set to 15, a Sub-type field (12 bits), followed by extension-specific data that the extension specification defines.

The Sub-type field is a 12-bit unique identifier that MUST be registered with IANA. This allows up to 4096 (0-4095) different sub-types, far exceeding the original packet type space. The exact structure of the extension-specific data portion is defined in each extension's specification document.
sections.eli5: The header has two parts: a 4-bit type field set to 15 (meaning 'shared extension'), and a 12-bit sub-type field that identifies which extension it is. After that comes the extension's own data format.

sections.title: IANA Registry for Packet Types and Sub-Types
sections.content:
This RFC creates a new IANA registry called 'LISP Packet Types' that formally lists packet type codes 0-15 and their assignments. The registry documents the original LISP message types (Map-Request, Map-Reply, Map-Register, Map-Notify, Encapsulated Control Message) and reserves type 15 for the shared extension.

For the shared extension type 15, a separate sub-registry was created: 'LISP Shared Extension Message Type Sub-types'. Sub-type values 0-1023 are assigned via Standards Action (requiring a Standards Track document), while values 1024-4095 are assigned via First Come, First Served (FCFS) basis. FCFS registrations require a point of contact and optionally a description of the extension's purpose.

The range values 5-7 and 9-14 in the main packet type registry remain available for future packet type allocations via Standards Action.
sections.eli5: IANA now keeps a registry listing all LISP packet types. For the new shared extension type, sub-types 0-1023 require formal standards approval, while 1024-4095 can be registered quickly on a first-come basis.

sections.title: Security and Status
sections.content:
This RFC is experimental and does not introduce security issues beyond those already present in RFC 6830. The shared extension message mechanism itself is neutral; security depends on how each extension uses the shared type.

Since this is an Experimental protocol, implementations should carefully validate sub-type fields and follow the specifications of the extension they are implementing. The centralized IANA registry helps prevent accidental duplication of sub-type codes.
sections.eli5: This RFC itself is just a mailbox management system. Security depends on what goes inside each envelope (extension). The registry prevents two extensions from using the same sub-type number by accident.
